title: Between the Lines: Decoding Signaling Differences in Public and Private Sector Job Advertisements
authors: Nico Gießmann; Nicolas Drathschmidt
affiliations: Institute of Human‐Centered Interactive Systems, University of Luebeck Lübeck Germany; Chair of Public and Nonprofit Management University of Potsdam Potsdam Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT To compete in the “war for talent,” public sector employers must demonstrate advantages over private employers. While public service motivation (PSM) predicts sector preference, scholars disagree on whether public employers (can) effectively signal PSM in job advertisements. Consequently, this article examines how public and private job advertisements differ in language. We collected 5000 advertisements from both sectors and performed natural language processing (NLP) and qualitative content analysis. Both sectors use specialized language that can narrow the applicant pool. PSM signals appear more often in the public sector, but affective motives are rarely communicated; instead, self‐sacrifice is framed as a legal obligation. Public sector advertisements adopt a rational tone instead of explaining purpose and societal value. Legally mandated, saturated signals may be perceived as low‐cost and ineffective. The findings explain the mixed results concerning PSM signaling and underscore the gap between theory and practice in PSM‐related recruitment efforts.

title: Steering and Setting Free: Insights From a 20‐Year Retrospective Case Study of a Security and Justice Organization's Digital Transformation
authors: Friso Selten; Dorus van Loo; Bram Klievink
affiliations: Institute of Public Administration, Leiden University The Hague the Netherlands
abstract: ABSTRACT Advances in digital technologies are expected to fundamentally change how organizations operate and create value. Empirical studies show that public organizations face difficulties organizing and sustaining this digital transformation. To better understand these challenges, this study examines the organizational mechanisms underlying digital transformation in a public organization over the past 20 years. Our findings show that this transformation was primarily enabled by an emergent change approach, with influential planned changes occurring only occasionally. We identify the organizational mechanisms underlying both types of change and analyze their interdependence. Our findings suggest that both emergent and planned change approaches may be needed to enable digital transformation in public organizations effectively, but that combining them is complex in practice.

title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
authors: Hale Erkan; Ashish Agarwal; Kumar Muthuraman; Ioannis Stamatopoulos
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States; The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, United States; University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information, Risk, and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States
abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
authors: Nathan Lawrence Justin; Sina Aghaei; Andres Gomez; Phebe Vayanos
affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California Viterbi School of Engineering, Industrial & Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
authors: Christian Füllner; Steffen Rebennack
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany; Karlsruher Institute of Technology (KIT), Institute of Operations Research, Karlsruhe, Germany
abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
authors: Markus Eyting
affiliations: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, 55128 Mainz, Germany; and Leibniz Institute for Financial Research Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe, 60323 Frankfurt am Main, Germany
abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
authors: Shashwat Agrawal; Nishant Kashyap; Sriniwas Mahapatro; Prasanna Tantri
affiliations: Department of Finance, Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Boston, Massachusetts 02467; Finance and Accounting Area, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, Vastrapur, Ahmedabad, Gujarat 380015, India; Department of Finance and Accounting, Saunders College of Business, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York 14623; Finance Area, Indian School of Business, Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Telangana 500032, India
abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
authors: Erdem Dogukan Yilmaz; Ivana Naumovska; Vikas A. Aggarwal
affiliations: INSEAD, 77305 Fontainebleau, France
abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

title: Social networks, institutional development, and entrepreneurship in China
authors: Jing Cai; Jun Du; Geoffrey Wood; Dayong Zhang
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, China; Aston University, UK; Western University, Canada; University of Bath, UK; City University of Macau, China
abstract: This paper explores how social network building, in functioning as an informal institutional mechanism, plays an important role in settings where rule-based formal institutions are incomplete or uneven in their coverage. Taking gift-giving as a proxy for social network investment, this study draws on a nationally representative household survey in China to examine its linkages with entrepreneurship. The results reveal a positive association between investing in social networks and both entrepreneurial participation and success. This relationship is statistically significant and robust against a battery of tests. By including regional institutional development in the empirical model, the interactions between different institutional layers are evaluated. Overall, this research indicates that stronger institutional development defines the boundary conditions of social network building in China.

title: Ambient Air Pollution Health Impacts in High‐Income Countries, Part II: A Case Study in the United Arab Emirates
authors: Tongchuan Wei; Nathan Ellermeier; Nick Kruskamp; Amal Mubarak Madhi; Latifa Juma Al Shamsi; Basema Ahmad Saddik; Jacqueline MacDonald Gibson
affiliations: Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA; Research Triangle Institute (RTI) International, Research Triangle Park North Carolina USA; Abu Dhabi Public Health Center Abu Dhabi UAE; Department of Public Health and Epidemiology, College of Medicine and Health Sciences Khalifa University Abu Dhabi UAE; School of Population Health, Faculty of Medicine University of New South Wales Sydney Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Ambient air pollution poses major global public health risks, particularly in rapidly developing regions, including the Arabian Gulf. This study estimates the disease burden attributable to anthropogenic air pollution (particulate matter [PM] and ozone) in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for 2019–2022 and compares findings to previous estimates for 2008. Burdens were calculated using updated air quality, population, and health incidence data for 2019–2022 along with concentration–response functions from recent epidemiologic evidence. Results show that Abu Dhabi's investments in air quality management have paid off in preventing air quality from deteriorating as much as would be expected given the doubling of the population between 2008 and 2022. However, epidemiologic evidence gathered during this period indicates that PM exposure has stronger negative effects on mortality risks than previously thought. As a result, estimated deaths attributable to anthropogenic ambient air pollution increased between 2008 and 2022, from 231 (90% uncertainty interval [UI]: 59–427) to 1249 (90% UI: 507–2169). Total hospital visits attributable to PM and ozone exposure also increased. These increases reflect combined effects of population growth, higher pollutant exposures, improved medical record‐keeping, and updated evidence on health risks. Urban centers, with higher pollutant concentrations and population densities, experience the highest risks, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address air pollution hotspots. This work provides policymakers with up‐to‐date insights on the health impacts of ambient air pollution and underscores the importance of continued investments in air quality management in Abu Dhabi.

title: Inseparability in Disaster Risk Science: Accounting for Coupled, Co‐Evolving Systems
authors: Alexandre Dunant; Stefan Hochrainer‐Stigler; Liz J Olaya Calderon; Ryan M. McGranaghan; Reinhard Mechler; Massimiliano Pittore; Sara M. Constantino; Silvia De Angeli; Marleen C. de Ruiter; Guillaume Falmagne; J. Camilo Gomez‐Zapata; Stefan Kienberger; Elco Koks; Elisabeth H. Krueger; Shahar Livne; Dora Elia Ramos Muñoz; Robert Šakić Trogrlić; PiaJohanna Schweizer; Thi Thu Ha Vo; Haorui Wu; Anqi Zhu
affiliations: Center for Climate Change and Transformation, Eurac Research Bolzano Italy; International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) Laxenburg Austria; Jet Propulsion Laboratory California Institute of Technology Pasadena California USA; Stanford University Stanford California USA; Université de Lorraine, CNRS, LIEC Metz France; Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM) Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam the Netherlands; Technological University Dublin Dublin Ireland; Trinity College Dublin Dublin Ireland; Climate Analytics Berlin Germany; GeoSphere Austria Salzburg Austria; Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics University of Amsterdam Amsterdam the Netherlands; Ben‐Gurion University of the Negev Beersheba Israel; El Colegio de la Frontera Sur (ECOSUR) San Cristóbal de las Casas Mexico; Research Institute for Sustainability (RIFS) GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences Potsdam Germany; School of Management Beijing Institute of Technology Beijing China; School of Social Work Dalhousie University Halifax Canada; Department of Geography Ludwig‐Maximilians‐Universität (LMU) Munich Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT Contemporary risk landscapes are shaped by systemic phenomena—compound disasters, cascading failures, non‐stationarity, and cross‐domain crises—that challenge conventional frameworks. While the classical risk equation (Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) remains a useful heuristic, it relies on a separability assumption that breaks down in feedback‐rich, co‐evolving systems. This failure reflects a familiar diagnosis: risk can be mistaken for a complicated problem, decomposable and optimizable, when it is a complex one, characterized by emergence and adaptation. Our contribution herein is not this distinction but its analytical consequence. Drawing on an interdisciplinary workshop on systemic risk and resilience, we propose inseparability as a foundational premise for disaster risk science. Hazard, exposure, and vulnerability might be better understood as dynamically coupled processes rather than separable variables. We derive implications across four axes: reframing vulnerability as a non‐ergodic system property; addressing cross‐scale dynamics; shifting from risk control to adaptive management; and treating knowledge co‐production as a scientific necessity.

title: Modeling Logical Interdependencies: Quantifying Systemic Risk From Rule‐Governed Actions
authors: Sukrati Gautam; David J. Yu; Hoon C. Shin; Mariam Alrefaei; Daniel Eisenberg; Changdeok Gim; Jeryang Park; Satish V. Ukkusuri
affiliations: Lyles School of Civil and Construction Engineering Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Ecological Sciences and Engineering Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Department of Political Science Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA; Division of Humanities and Social Sciences Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH) Pohang Republic of Korea; Environmental Engineering and Sustainability Department College of Engineering and Energy Abdullah Al Salem University Kuwait City Kuwait; Department of Operations Research Naval Postgraduate School Monterey California USA; Department of Technology and Society State University of New York Incheon Republic of Korea; Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering Hongik University Seoul Republic of Korea; Department of Computer Science Purdue University West Lafayette Indiana USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic risk in critical infrastructure is often analyzed through physical, geographic, and cyber interdependencies. Yet infrastructures are also interdependent through the governing rules that organize human action. These rule‐mediated connections are a form of logical interdependency, and breakdowns in rule‐governed action can create pathways through which disruption spreads. This paper develops a framework for diagnosing and quantifying this underrecognized source of systemic risk. It does so by modeling logical interdependencies as rule‐mediated control relations that shape whether interconnected infrastructures remain within safe operating bounds or drift toward failure. Integrating Institutional Grammar, STAMP, and Bayesian inference, the framework translates governing rules into structured control relations, represents them within a socio‐technical control architecture, and quantifies how failures in those relations propagate across interconnected infrastructures. We demonstrate the framework through a reservoir system case study centered on Lake Mendocino, California, where safety depends not only on reservoir infrastructure and hydrologic conditions, but also on distributed authority, communication requirements, and operational protocols. The results show that logical interdependencies make non‐trivial contributions to modeled systemic risk, with baseline probabilities of 7% for Coyote Valley Dam failure and 3% for downstream community impacts under the modeled conditions. More importantly, the analysis reveals hidden logical risk : rules and control relations that appear routine in normal operation yet become disproportionately important when the Bayesian model traces which factors most strongly contribute to a failure scenario. The paper moves logical interdependencies from a residual conceptual category to a systematically identifiable and quantitatively analyzable pathway of systemic risk.

title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
authors: Jan C Fransoo; Guan-Yuan Wang; Simone Balvers
affiliations: Tilburg University
abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

title: Inter-organisational Capabilities and the Transformation of Trust in Blockchain-based Smart Contracts: A Framework for SME Ecosystems
authors: Maksym Koghut; Cathy Urquhart; Soo Hee Lee; Omar Al-Tabbaa
affiliations: University of Kent; Manchester Metropolitan University - All Saints Campus; University of Leeds
abstract: Blockchain-based smart contracts embed agreement enforcement within executable code, constraining the partner discretion that inter-organisational relationships (IORs) have traditionally coordinated through trust, communication, and relational governance. This raises a question that popular accounts tend to foreclose: whether automated enforcement makes inter-organisational trust unnecessary, or whether trust instead changes in function and object. Drawing on expert consultation with 28 blockchain specialists and 25 in-depth interviews with executives, we conduct an inductive study of how IORs transform as organisations adopt smart contracts. We develop a framework in which intensive relational exchange enables organisations to build two inter-organisational capabilities, Distributed Transparency Capability and Algorithmic Coordination Capability, through which they actualise the affordances that smart contracts offer. Through this capability development a distinctive inter-organisational trust form emerges, System-based Trust, defined as warranted reliance on coordinating infrastructure that partner organisations jointly construct. System-based Trust complements rather than replaces relational trust: it carries operational coordination and frees relational trust for strategic collaboration and exception handling, producing Hybrid Inter-organisational Relationships as the outcome of successful transformation. The framework applies to small and medium-sized enterprise ecosystems with limited numbers of trading partners; larger-scale consortia and power-asymmetric networks fall outside its scope. Our findings reposition smart contracts as occasions for capability development rather than substitutes for inter-organisational trust.

title: Designing Liminal Spaces for Upstream Performativity: Lessons From The Futures Lab
authors: Annmarie Ryan
affiliations: Kemmy Business School, University of Limerick Limerick Ireland
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how business schools can function as liminal socio‐material infrastructures for upstream performative experimentation. Recent work has advanced management scholarship to foreground the role of imagination in theorizing for desirable futures. However, less is understood about how alternatives might be made sufficiently tangible and credible to acquire performative force in the first place. This is compounded by performativity research that has largely examined how theories acquire effects once they circulate in markets and organizations. To address this, and drawing on a 5‐year qualitative case study of The Futures Lab (TFL), I show how shared visual workspaces, repeated critique, direct engagement with stakeholders, and the making and remaking of maps, models and prototypes enabled participants to (re)‐search alternative futures by making possibilities visible, contestable and open to revision. These practices produced credible fictions: tangible yet provisional representations to which external actors could attach, align with, and sometimes enrol around emerging possibilities. I develop prefigurative theorizing as a materially experimental mode of prospective theorizing, showing how desirable futures gain performative force not through imagination alone, but by being externalized, provisionally enacted, tested and revised in the present. The study thereby specifies conditions through which business schools can cultivate upstream performativity.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
authors: Andy Wu; Ronald Wang
affiliations: Strategy Unit, Harvard Business School Harvard University Boston Massachusetts USA; Department of Management Science and Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: Issue Information
Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
authors: Sung Ho Park; Alex Murray
affiliations: Department of Management, Lundquist College of Business University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

title: Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
authors: Gary Dushnitsky
affiliations: Strategy & Entrepreneurship Area London Business School London UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

title: Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
authors: Rogerio Santarrosa
affiliations: Insper Institute of Education and Research ,
abstract: Abstract Civil wars are a recurring phenomenon undermining development in weak states. Faced with the possibility of costly conflict, why don’t leaders share power? I investigate the role of an unexplored commitment problem, both theoretically and empirically. The model features a leader who can appease challengers by sharing power, but doing so increases their effectiveness at launching a rebellion. I show that commitment worsens as the opposition becomes stronger, and derive testable non-monotonic implications of group strength on power-sharing and conflict. As challengers become stronger, the likelihood of inclusion (positive transfers) increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader prefers to exclude an opposing group and face conflict. I test the model using data on politically relevant ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, their access to executive power, and on armed organizations that claim to represent them. I use within-country variation in population share to proxy for group strength. The empirical findings strongly accord with the predictions of the theory. I then structurally estimate the model parameters and explore policy-relevant counterfactuals, including the effects of democratization, changes in military capacity, financial aid, sanctions, and quotas.

title: The Dynamics of the Racial Wealth Gap
authors: Dionissi Aliprantis; Daniel R. Carroll; Eric R. Young
affiliations: ENS de Lyon Lyon France; Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Cleveland Ohio USA; University of Virginia Charlottesville Virginia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race. We find that equalizing earnings is critical for permanent reductions in racial wealth inequality, and that one‐time transfers will have only transitory effects unless earnings are also equalized. Our results are robust to the introduction of racial differences in returns to saving, which only matter after earnings inequality is reduced.

title: PROXIMAL ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE
authors: Alberto Quaini; Fabio Trojani
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Geneva, Swiss Finance Institute, and Collegio Carlo Alberto
abstract: Abstract We develop a convex-analytic framework for constructing and analyzing a broad class of penalized estimators. Our method defines penalized estimators by applying proximal operators to benchmark estimators, rather than by penalizing the benchmark criterion itself. We establish general finite-sample properties, derive unified asymptotic distribution results, and provide tractable conditions for oracle selection and oracle asymptotic efficiency. We then apply the framework to linear regression with irregular designs, including singular and nearly-singular cases. In this setting, where the coefficient vector need not be point identified, we motivate the Ridgeless estimand as the inferential target, construct a n $\sqrt {n}$ StartRoot n EndRoot -consistent modified Ridgeless benchmark estimator, and combine it with adaptive proximal penalization to obtain, to the best of our knowledge, the first penalized estimator achieving the oracle property under both regular and irregular designs.

title: When Acknowledgements Don’t Match: Evidence from Horizon 2020
authors: Matthias Müller
abstract: Abstract Funding acknowledgements have become a valuable data source in recent years. The validity of acknowledgements as indicators of direct project-level support, however, remains contested for several reasons. This study examines the reliability of funding acknowledgement data by comparing publications that acknowledge the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Framework Programme in Scopus with publications officially recorded as project outputs in the CORDIS database. Focusing on social science–related fields, this study conducts aggregate-, project-, and semantic-level analyses to assess the correspondence between acknowledged and administratively recorded funding. The results show a substantial and persistent mismatch: only about half of the publications acknowledging Horizon 2020 funding in Scopus can be linked to a corresponding project in CORDIS. This divergence is persistent over time, occurs across funding instruments and subject areas, and is unlikely to be explained solely by reporting delays, administrative incompleteness, or technical matching limitations alone. Instead, the semantic analysis indicates that many unmatched publications are thematically more distant from the confirmed research core of funded projects, suggesting that funding acknowledgements in bibliographic metadata capture also broader, indirect, or non-project-core relations to funding beyond formally reported project outputs.

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
authors: MICHELE BISCEGLIA; ALESSIO PICCOLO; JAN SCHNEEMEIER
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
authors: Brant E. Christensen; Nathan G. Lundstrom; Nathan J. Newton
affiliations: Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA; University of Kansas Lawrence Kansas USA; Florida State University Tallahassee Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

title: Spatiality of preemptive coercion: How autocrats demolish informal settlements for political control
authors: Shiqi Ma
affiliations: Department of Politics and International Studies SOAS University of London London United Kingdom
abstract: Abstract Why do authorities demolish informal settlements in metropolises? The social sciences have a long tradition of addressing this issue through the lens of economic development or welfare provision. I instead propose a theory of political control. Autocrats adopt demolition as a preemptive and coercive tool to remove communities substantively and symbolically less legible to them, thereby ensuring societal compliance and restoring visual order. Empirically, I compile a unique dataset of 320 demolished and undemolished informal settlements in Beijing between 2017 and 2018, based on satellite imagery, digital street views, and fieldwork. The results indicate that the low legibility of informal settlements to authorities correlates with a greater likelihood of demolition. This paper contributes to the social science literature by connecting legibility politics with urban governance. It also introduces a spatial perspective and leverages novel data sources to deepen our understanding of preemptive coercion under authoritarianism.
